svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. How two identities actually get linked today
svg.desc: Five linkage paths between a personal identity and a research identity. The third-party cookie path is marked as largely closed in browsers that block third-party cookies by default. Four paths remain open: the device fingerprint, the network address, activity timing, and any account you sign in to. A note explains that the classic pixel-and-cookie story is the one everyone teaches and the one least likely to be how it happens now.
svg.text: Figure 2: Five Paths Between Two Identities
One of these is the path every guide describes. It is also the one most likely to be closed already.
PERSONAL
signed in, named,
unremarkable
RESEARCH
no accounts, and
meant to stay apart
1. A third-party cookie, read on both sites
Largely closed where third-party cookies are blocked by default, which is Safari, Firefox and Brave. Still open in Chrome.
2. The device fingerprint
Same machine, same graphics, same fonts. Lesson 2.2 measured this. Containers and profiles do nothing about it.
3. The network address
One connection, one address, both identities. Figure 1 shows that no layer of compartmentalization touches this.
4. Timing
Personal activity stops, research activity starts, minutes apart, every day. Lesson 1.3 covered timing as an identifier.
5. You sign in to something
One account, once, in the wrong window. No technical control survives this, and it is the way it usually happens.
Path 1 is the story everybody tells. Paths 2 to 5 are the ones you have to plan for.
Compartmentalization by cookies closes a path that your browser may have closed already. It leaves the other four untouched, and the last one is not a technical problem at all.
